lessonRef.subject: ready-for-life
lessonRef.title: Unit performance task: receiving and acting on feedback

objective: Learners respond to two provided fictional pieces of workplace feedback, one easy to accept and one genuinely difficult, drafting a professional response to each and a short written response accepting and acting on the harder one, then justify the communication choices made across this unit's work, completing the unit's performance task.
scenario: The learner reads two provided fictional feedback messages, one straightforward and one that is difficult to hear (specific and somewhat critical but professionally delivered), drafts a brief professional response to each that neither over-apologizes nor gets defensive, and writes a short justification connecting this response to at least one other message drafted earlier in the unit.
safetyNotes: Both feedback messages are fictional and provided with this lesson; no real supervisor, workplace, or evaluation of the learner personally is involved.
materials: the two provided fictional feedback messages

tasks.directions: Read both feedback messages and note your honest first reaction to each, especially the harder one.

prompts.text: Describe your honest first reaction to the harder feedback message, before drafting a response.

tasks.directions: Draft a brief professional response to each feedback message.

prompts.text: Draft your response to the straightforward feedback.
Draft your response to the harder feedback, naming one specific thing you'll do differently, without over-apologizing or getting defensive.
My response to the harder feedback names a specific action, not just an acknowledgment.

tasks.directions: Justify your communication choices by connecting this response to at least one other message you drafted earlier in the unit.

prompts.text: Name one specific choice from this response (a wording choice, structural choice, or tone choice) and connect it to something you learned drafting a different message earlier this unit.

tasks.directions: Reflect on receiving difficult feedback overall.

prompts.text: What is the difference between accepting feedback and agreeing that you're a bad person, and how does your response show that difference?

remediation: If a learner's response to the harder feedback is either purely apologetic with no named action, or defensive and explaining why the feedback is wrong, reteach using a three-part pattern (acknowledge the specific point, name one concrete action, close without over-apologizing) modeled once on the easier feedback message before revising the harder response.
extension: Have the learner draft a short follow-up message to send after acting on the feedback for one week, reporting back on the specific change made.
